title: 2 Kings 3:1–12
context: Chapter 3 introduces Jehoram son of Ahab, king of Israel, who is distinct from Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah (2 Kings 8:16). The narrator gives him a mixed verdict: he removes the pillar of Baal his father made but holds to the sins of Jeroboam. The dating in the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat does not align simply with 2 Kings 1:17, and interpreters often propose overlapping reigns, though the reconstruction remains uncertain. When Mesha king of Moab stops paying tribute after Ahab’s death (compare 2 Kings 1:1), Jehoram enlists Jehoshaphat of Judah and the king of Edom. The narrator does not explain why the route through the wilderness of Edom was chosen. After seven days without water, Jehoram despairs, while Jehoshaphat asks for a prophet of the LORD, and the kings go down to Elisha. Both traditions read the scene as a turn from human strategy to dependence on the LORD’s word.

verses.text: Now Jehoram the son of Ahab began to reign over Israel in Samaria in the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, and reigned twelve years.
verses.arminianNotes: The verse dates Jehoram’s reign by the reign of Jehoshaphat of Judah, tying the northern and southern kingdoms together in one story. Arminian readers note that each new king receives a real opportunity to lead Israel back to the LORD, and the twelve years that follow will show how Jehoram uses the reign entrusted to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the regnal formula as a reminder that kings rise and fall within the LORD’s governance of history, even in the northern kingdom. Both traditions agree that this Jehoram, son of Ahab, is distinct from Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat of Judah (2 Kings 8:16), and that the narrator is setting the stage for God’s dealings with both royal houses.

verses.text: He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, but not like his father and like his mother, for he put away the pillar of Baal that his father had made.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers appreciate the narrator’s careful evaluation: Jehoram did evil, yet not like Ahab and Jezebel, since he put away the pillar of Baal his father had made. Partial reform is genuinely noticed, showing that God weighs real differences in human conduct even when a life falls short of wholehearted faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the measured verdict and see it as evidence that God restrains evil even in a wicked dynasty, so that one king’s removal of a Baal pillar is a mercy to Israel. Both traditions agree that outward reform without a heart turned to the LORD still leaves a king under the narrator’s judgment of evil.

verses.text: Nevertheless he held to the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, with which he made Israel to sin. He didn’t depart from them.
verses.arminianNotes: The sins of Jeroboam, the golden calves at Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:28–30), remain the standard charge against northern kings. Arminian readers stress that Jehoram held to these sins and did not depart from them, which presents his failure as a persistent choice, and they invite readers to examine where they too hold on to compromise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize how deeply rooted the sin of Jeroboam had become, shaping king after king, and they see in it the grip of entrenched idolatry on a nation’s heart. Both traditions agree that removing Baal while keeping the calves is an incomplete repentance, and that the LORD’s verdict rests on whole loyalty rather than selective reform.

verses.text: Now Mesha king of Moab was a sheep breeder; and he supplied the king of Israel with one hundred thousand lambs and the wool of one hundred thousand rams.
verses.arminianNotes: Mesha’s tribute of lambs and wool shows that Moab had been a vassal paying a heavy levy to Israel. Arminian readers note that the narrator records economic and political realities plainly, and that the coming war arises from ordinary human motives such as the desire for independence, within which God will still act.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that even tribute and trade fall within the providence that governs nations, and that Moab’s subjection had been part of Israel’s place among its neighbors. Both traditions agree that the verse explains the stakes of the rebellion and introduces Mesha as a real ruler with his own interests, not a mere backdrop to Israel’s story.

verses.text: But when Ahab was dead, the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The rebellion after Ahab’s death picks up the note already sounded in 2 Kings 1:1. Arminian readers see a pattern in Kings in which changes of leadership open space for neighbors to test Israel, and they note that Israel’s weakened faithfulness has real consequences for its standing among the nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same pattern and read it partly as covenant discipline, since the books of Kings often link Israel’s troubles with its unfaithfulness. Both traditions agree that the narrator does not state a direct cause for the timing here, and they are careful not to claim more than the text says while recognizing that God is not absent from these events.

verses.text: King Jehoram went out of Samaria at that time, and mustered all Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehoram responds by mustering all Israel, a decisive and practical step. Arminian readers note that the king acts on his own counsel without first seeking the LORD, a contrast that becomes sharp when Jehoshaphat later asks for a prophet, and they see human initiative without inquiry of God shown to be insufficient.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that Jehoram plans and mobilizes before seeking the LORD, and they see the following crisis as God’s way of exposing the limits of human strategy. Both traditions agree that the verse does not condemn military preparation as such, but sets up a story in which deliverance will come only through the LORD’s word.

verses.text: He went and sent to Jehoshaphat the king of Judah, saying, “The king of Moab has rebelled against me. Will you go with me against Moab to battle?” He said, “I will go up. I am as you are, my people as your people, my horses as your horses.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jehoshaphat answers with words of full solidarity, echoing his earlier alliance with Ahab (1 Kings 22:4). Arminian readers note that a godly king freely chooses a costly partnership with an unfaithful house, and the story invites reflection on the risks of alliances that may compromise faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly recall that Jehoshaphat was rebuked for helping the wicked in an earlier alliance (2 Chronicles 19:2), and they see a similar pattern here. Both traditions agree that Jehoshaphat is portrayed as a genuine believer who nevertheless makes questionable choices, and that God will still show him mercy within the consequences of those choices.

verses.text: Then he said, “Which way shall we go up?” Jehoram answered, “The way of the wilderness of Edom.”
verses.arminianNotes: The decision to march by the way of the wilderness of Edom is presented as a strategic choice, and the text does not explain the reasoning behind it. Arminian readers note that the route is chosen by human planning, and that the hardship that follows tests the wisdom of that plan and the faith of those who made it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the narrator gives the route without stating its purpose, and they see in what follows how God governs even the paths that human leaders choose for themselves. Both traditions agree it is best not to supply a strategy the text does not give, and that the route sets up the crisis of water that drives the kings to seek the LORD’s word.

verses.text: So the king of Israel went with the king of Judah and the king of Edom, and they marched for seven days along a circuitous route. There was no water for the army or for the animals that followed them.
verses.arminianNotes: Seven days of circuitous marching leave the army and its animals without water, a crisis that threatens the whole coalition. Arminian readers see in this a moment when human plans reach their limit, and they emphasize that such moments press people to turn to the LORD in genuine, freely offered dependence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the lack of water as part of God’s providence, bringing the kings to the end of their resources so that the deliverance to come will plainly be his work. Both traditions agree that the verse joins the king of Edom to the alliance and highlights a real physical need, which the LORD will meet in an unexpected way.

verses.text: The king of Israel said, “Alas! For the LORD has called these three kings together to deliver them into the hand of Moab.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jehoram’s cry interprets the crisis as the LORD’s hostile intent, yet he does not seek the LORD’s word. Arminian readers note that he acknowledges God’s involvement only in a fatalistic way, and that such resignation differs sharply from the trusting inquiry that Jehoshaphat models in the next verse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jehoram rightly senses that the LORD governs events but wrongly concludes that God intends only destruction. Both traditions agree that the verse shows how a troubled conscience can misread divine providence, and that the true meaning of the LORD’s purposes is learned through his prophetic word rather than through fear.

verses.text: But Jehoshaphat said, “Isn’t there a prophet of the LORD here, that we may inquire of the LORD by him?” One of the king of Israel’s servants answered, “Elisha the son of Shaphat, who poured water on the hands of Elijah, is here.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jehoshaphat asks whether a prophet of the LORD is present, as he did before the battle at Ramoth Gilead (1 Kings 22:7). Arminian readers commend his instinct to seek God’s word, and they note that the description of Elisha as the one who poured water on Elijah’s hands recalls the faithful service that prepared him for his calling (1 Kings 19:19–21).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers highlight that God had already placed his prophet within reach of the army before the kings knew to ask, and they see providence in Elisha’s presence. Both traditions agree that Elisha’s credentials rest on his relationship with Elijah and on the LORD’s call, and that the narrative honors humble service as preparation for ministry.

verses.text: Jehoshaphat said, “The LORD’s word is with him.” So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat and the king of Edom went down to him.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehoshaphat affirms that the LORD’s word is with Elisha, and the three kings go down to him rather than summoning him. Arminian readers note the humility of this movement and see it as a fitting response to God’s word, which invites people of every rank to come and hear it for themselves.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that the authority of the LORD’s word places kings beneath the prophet in this scene, since they must come to him. Both traditions agree that the verse turns the story from human strategy to divine revelation, and that the dignity of the prophet derives entirely from the word God has entrusted to him.
